subtype: Approach: dreaming up ideas and then choosing one [Thinking]
passage: Ira tore a page from her rough notebook and wrote three headings: clue hunt, movie night, pizza evening. Her birthday was in six days, and the flat had only two rooms. Under each idea she scribbled what it would need. Pizza would cost the most, and ten friends would never fit around the table. A movie needed the sofa, and half the guests would sit on the floor and grow restless. "But a clue hunt," she muttered, "lives in the hallway, the balcony, under the beds." Her brother Omkar peeked over her shoulder. "Can I hide the clues?" "Yes," said Ira, and circled the first heading twice.

qa.q: How many days were left until Ira's birthday?
qa.a: Her birthday was in six days.

qa.q: What was Ira feeling as she circled the first heading twice?
qa.a: Ira seemed pleased and decided; the way she muttered and circled shows she had weighed each idea and felt sure about the clue hunt. 😊

qa.q: What alternative approach could Ira use to choose, and why might it work?
qa.a: Ira could ask a few friends which idea they would enjoy most, because guests know what is fun for them. She could also check the plan with a parent to be sure it fits the budget.

qa.q: How might Omkar see the plan for the party?
qa.a: Omkar seems excited because Omkar asks to hide the clues, so the hunt gives a brother a real job in the celebration.

grounding: A girl brainstorms three party ideas, compares them for cost, space and fun, and chooses the one that suits the small flat.

subtype: Approach: writing a to-do list and dividing jobs at home [Action]
passage: Only three days remained, and Chinmay had a pencil, a sheet of paper and a problem. He wrote a list: cake, invitations, decorations, games. Then he called his family to the table. "Mahima didi, can you order the cake with Papa?" "Fine," said his sister. "Mummy, decorations?" "I have old streamers," she said. His little brother took the games. Chinmay kept invitations for himself, because he loved to draw. That evening he drew a rocket on every card, folded each one and wrote a name inside. By the second night nine were done, and only the glue stick was missing. He checked the item off with a smile.

qa.q: Which job did Chinmay keep for himself?
qa.a: Chinmay kept the invitations.

qa.q: Why did Chinmay keep the invitations for himself?
qa.a: Chinmay loves to draw, so this job suited him and let him enjoy the work.

qa.q: What alternative approach could help if a helper does not finish a job, and why?
qa.a: Chinmay could check in halfway through the three days and swap a job that is behind. Seeing the list often helps everyone notice what is late in time to fix it.

qa.q: How might Mahima see being asked to order the cake?
qa.a: Mahima probably feels trusted and included; being handed a real task means the party is a shared effort and not only Chinmay's.

grounding: A boy lists the cake, invitations, decorations and games and gives family members a job each, keeping the drawn invitations for himself.

subtype: Approach: planning only the fun parts and ignoring food and time [Pitfall]
passage: I'm Ishita. For my tenth birthday I planned five games: musical chairs, pass the parcel, a treasure trail, a balloon race and dumb charades. I wrote them on a card and felt very organised. I did not write when the cake would be cut, or who would eat what. On the day, nobody had eaten since lunch, and by five o'clock two friends were sitting on the stairs with sad faces. The charades had not even started when the doorbell rang and parents began arriving. Jomon's mother waited at the door with her scooter keys. My party ended with half the games unplayed and me feeling terrible.

qa.q: How many games did Ishita plan?
qa.a: Ishita planned five games.

qa.q: How did Ishita feel when the party ended with half the games unplayed?
qa.a: Ishita felt terrible and probably disappointed, since the plan looked good on the card but did not work on the day.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Ishita use next time, and why?
qa.a: Ishita could write a time for each activity and put snacks in the plan, because a schedule shows if the games fit before parents come. Ishita could ask a parent to look over the plan.

qa.q: How might Jomon's mother see the party running late?
qa.a: Jomon's mother waited at the door with scooter keys, so the delay probably felt inconvenient and worrying, especially if the parent did not know how long the games would take.

grounding: A girl plans five games but forgets snacks and timings, so the guests are hungry and the games run past pick-up time.

subtype: Approach: preparing a plan B in case it rains [Thinking]
passage: Sunday, 9 pm. Party plan for Saturday: the park near our building, cricket, a picnic mat, and a cake in the shade. I felt so proud of it. Then Ammi's phone buzzed with a weather message and I thought: what if it rains? Twelve friends, one wet cake, no place to go. I sat with my pencil for ten minutes. Answer: push the sofa against the wall, roll up the carpet, and play indoor games like passing the parcel and a quiz. Pradeep can bring his speaker. Now the party happens either way. I'm going to write BOTH plans on one page tonight. Rafiq.

qa.q: Where will the party be held if the weather is good?
qa.a: The party will be in the park near Rafiq's building.

qa.q: What did Rafiq worry about after the weather message?
qa.a: Rafiq worried that rain would leave twelve friends and a wet cake with no place to go.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Rafiq use to make the plan stronger, and why?
qa.a: Rafiq could pick a date with a backup day or ask the friends' families which they prefer. A second option protects the celebration so it does not have to be cancelled.

qa.q: How might Pradeep see the indoor plan?
qa.a: Pradeep is given a job, bringing the speaker, so the indoor plan probably feels like a real part of the party and not a second-best.

grounding: A boy plans a park party, asks what if it rains, and prepares an indoor plan so the celebration is not cancelled.

subtype: Approach: imagining the party hour by hour in his head [Thinking]
passage: I closed my eyes on the bus and walked through my party like a film. Friends arrive at four, shoes off. We play musical statues at half past four. Cake at five. Everyone leaves at six. Then I saw Ira in the corner of my mind, by herself, holding a glass of juice. She barely knows anyone from my class. I opened my eyes. My plan had nothing for her. So I added a team game where everybody gets a role: one holds the map, one reads clues, one runs. Nobody can hide in a corner. I'm glad I checked it in my head first. Ramya.

qa.q: What time does the cake come in the plan?
qa.a: The cake comes at five.

qa.q: What does Ramya notice while imagining the party, and what might Ramya feel about it?
qa.a: Ramya notices the plan has nothing for Ira, who is alone and barely knows anyone, and probably feels concerned and thoughtful about making everyone comfortable.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Ramya use to test the plan, and why?
qa.a: Ramya could tell the plan to a parent or an older cousin and ask what they see missing. Another person may spot a gap that Ramya's own picture leaves out.

qa.q: How does the party look from Ira's point of view?
qa.a: Ira barely knows anyone from Ramya's class, so the party as first planned would look lonely; with a role in the team game, Ira would have a reason to join in.

grounding: A girl imagines the party hour by hour, spots that shy guests have nothing to do and adds a team game with a role for everyone.

subtype: Approach: checking the budget with a parent and trimming [Revision]
passage:
Monday. Dolma wrote the party list: balloons, return gifts, cake. At the stationery shop and the bakery, Dolma noted each price on the back of a copybook.

Wednesday. Dolma showed the numbers to Ama. She counted the money in the envelope she had set aside and shook her head. "This is more than we can spend, Dolma." Dolma stared at the page, then crossed out the fancy gift bags. "Small pencil sets instead. And I'll cut coloured paper for the decorations."

Saturday. Paper chains hung across the room. The pencil sets went home in twelve hands, and Ama's envelope still had a little money left.

qa.q: What did Dolma give the guests as return gifts in the end?
qa.a: Dolma gave small pencil sets.

qa.q: How did Dolma feel when Ama shook her head over the prices?
qa.a: Dolma was probably disappointed, since Dolma stared at the page in silence before crossing out the fancy gift bags, but Dolma stayed practical. 😔

qa.q: What alternative approach could Dolma use to plan the spending, and why?
qa.a: Dolma could set the limit first and choose what fits inside it, since deciding the total before shopping avoids the shock of adding it up later.

qa.q: How might Ama see Dolma's changes to the plan?
qa.a: Ama likely sees a child who listened and worked with a limit; the envelope had money left, so Ama may feel relieved and proud.

grounding: When the costs exceed the envelope, the child checks with Ama and trims the return gifts and decorations to fit.

subtype: Approach: insisting on copying a friend's grand party [Pitfall]
passage: I'm Rehana, and I live next door to Shankar. On Monday at recess he told everyone about a classmate's party with a magician and a huge bouncy castle. "Mine will be exactly like that," he said. On Tuesday, through the wall, I heard his father say it was too much for the family. Shankar shut his door hard and skipped dinner. On Wednesday he sat on the stairs, staring, and said nothing about the party for two days. Then I saw him drawing on an old calendar page: cricket in the lane, a big chocolate cake, everyone's names. "This is what I actually like," he told me.

qa.q: What did Shankar want at his party?
qa.a: Shankar wanted a bouncy castle and a magician like a classmate's party.

qa.q: What was Shankar feeling after his father said it was too much for the family?
qa.a: Shankar was upset and disappointed; shutting the door hard, skipping dinner and staring silently on the stairs all point to it. 😔

qa.q: What alternative approach could Shankar use, and why?
qa.a: Shankar could start with what he enjoys and what the family can afford, and then add one special touch. A plan that fits the family means less arguing and more fun.

qa.q: How does Rehana see what happens to Shankar?
qa.a: Rehana watches from next door and hears the argument, so Rehana sees a neighbour go from sulking to planning and seems relieved when Shankar shares the drawing.

grounding: A boy insists on copying a classmate's grand party, the family cannot afford it and he is upset until he plans around his own favourites.

subtype: Approach: changing the game when guests look bored [Revision]
passage:
Friday. Disha wrote her birthday plan: a game with chairs, quiet and neat, and cake after. She liked how tidy it looked.

Saturday. Ten friends sat in a ring. Two minutes in, Meera was yawning, someone kept peeking at the garden, and a boy tapped his feet. Disha looked around and put the whistle down. "New game! Catch the ribbon in the garden!" The chairs stayed in the hall and everybody ran outside, shouting.

Sunday. Gopika phoned. "That garden game was the best part. Can we play it at my house?"

qa.q: What did Disha change the game to when the chairs stopped working?
qa.a: Disha switched to catching the ribbon in the garden.

qa.q: What did Disha notice about her friends during the quiet game, and what might Disha feel?
qa.a: Disha noticed yawning, peeking at the garden and tapping feet; Disha probably felt worried the party was going flat but decided quickly.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Disha have used, and why?
qa.a: Disha could have prepared one quiet and one active game in advance, so a switch would be easy. Having a spare game means the party need not depend on a single idea.

qa.q: What did the change mean for Gopika?
qa.a: Gopika enjoyed the garden game most and wants to play it again, so for Gopika the switch saved the afternoon.

grounding: At the party the quiet game falls flat, so the birthday girl notices restless friends and changes to an active game outdoors.

subtype: Approach: calming down before deciding what to do [Thinking]
passage:
Hemant: Zoya, you're still glaring at me. It was only a pen.
Zoya: Don't talk to me right now. My face is hot. If I speak, I'll say something mean.
Hemant: So what will you do?
Zoya: I'll read my book till lunch is over. Later, when I'm not shaking, I'll think about it properly.
Hemant: That's your whole plan?
Zoya: If I answer now it becomes a bigger fight. Later I can work out if I'm angry about the pen or about how you grabbed it.
Hemant: Fine. I'll be under the tree.
Zoya: Good. Not yet, Hemant.

qa.q: Where will Hemant wait while Zoya reads?
qa.a: Hemant will wait under the tree.

qa.q: What is Zoya feeling when Zoya's face turns hot?
qa.a: Zoya is angry and afraid of saying something mean, and wants to stay quiet until the feeling passes.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Zoya use later, and why?
qa.a: Zoya could tell Hemant calmly how the grabbing felt and ask what happened, since a calm talk lets both explain. Working out what actually happened is another way forward.

qa.q: How does Hemant see Zoya's silence?
qa.a: Hemant may find it hard to be told to wait, but agreeing to sit under the tree shows a willingness to give space instead of pushing.

grounding: After a fight over a borrowed pen, Zoya feels hot with anger and decides to stay quiet and think once calmer.

subtype: Approach: working out what actually happened [Thinking]
passage: That night Kabir lay on his bed, replaying Tuesday. His friend Farhan's tiffin had slipped off the desk and the rice went everywhere. Kabir had laughed, loudly. Farhan had gone very still, then shouted, "You always mock me!" and marched off to the playground. Kabir's first thought was: he's overreacting, it was funny. But he ran the scene back slowly. Farhan on his knees, picking rice out of the dust. The whole class watching. And Kabir's laugh, the loudest one. He sat up. If that were his own tiffin, he would be furious too. Tomorrow he would not start with "you were unfair." He would start with what he had done.

qa.q: What did Kabir do when Farhan's tiffin fell?
qa.a: Kabir laughed loudly.

qa.q: How did Kabir's thinking change as he replayed the scene?
qa.a: Kabir first thought Farhan was overreacting, then felt guilty and understood how mocked Farhan must have felt.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Kabir try tomorrow, and why?
qa.a: Kabir could say sorry for the laugh and explain there was no mean intention, because the hurt comes first. Offering to help or share lunch could also show care.

qa.q: How does the moment look to Farhan?
qa.a: Farhan was kneeling in front of the class, picking up rice, and heard the loudest laugh from Kabir, so it felt like being mocked by a friend.

grounding: A boy replays the quarrel, realises his laugh at the dropped tiffin felt like mockery and sees the friend's side.
